## Vision

Kiln is the open-source answer to a simple question: what if your AI model got better every time you used it?

Today, serving and training are separate worlds. You deploy a model, discover its failures, collect examples, upload them to some training service, wait hours, redeploy, and hope. Kiln collapses that entire cycle into a single API call. You submit corrections or scored completions, and the model improves in seconds — while continuing to serve requests without interruption.

The core insight: a 4B parameter model, purpose-tuned to YOUR specific workloads via continuous LoRA adaptation, will outperform a generic 70B model on the tasks you actually care about. And it runs on hardware you already own.

## Why This Wins

**Lock-in through excellence, not walls.** Once you've trained Kiln on thousands of your domain-specific examples — your code style, your data formats, your edge cases, your preferences — switching to anything else means starting over. The model becomes irreplaceable not because we lock you in, but because your accumulated training data and adapted weights are genuinely valuable. This is the most ethical form of lock-in: the product is simply too good at YOUR job to replace.

**The 4B sweet spot.** Large enough to be genuinely capable. Small enough to run on a single consumer GPU (RTX 3090/4090, 24GB). Small enough that LoRA training completes in seconds, not hours. Small enough that continuous batching handles dozens of concurrent requests. This is the Goldilocks zone for self-hosted AI.

**Single-model, zero-abstraction.** Every line of code is tuned for one model architecture. No plugin systems, no abstraction layers, no "supports 47 model families." The scheduler knows exactly how much KV cache each layer needs. The block manager is sized for this model's GQA configuration. The training loop knows the exact parameter count. This specificity is the source of speed.

**Pure Rust, single process.** No Python sidecar. No second copy of the model. Training happens in-process on the already-loaded model using Rust ML libraries (candle, tch). One process, one model in memory, one binary to deploy. A Python sidecar is acceptable ONLY as a future fallback for exotic training regimes that don't have Rust implementations yet — never the primary path.

**Training as a first-class API.** Not a separate tool. Not a notebook. Not a CLI that runs overnight. POST your examples to /v1/train/sft or your scored completions to /v1/train/grpo, and the model improves. The GRPO loop — generate, score, train, serve — runs against a single server with a single API.

## Technical Architecture

```
Single Rust binary (kiln):
  - axum HTTP server (OpenAI-compatible + training + adapter APIs)
  - Iteration-level scheduler (Sarathi-style chunked prefill)
  - Block manager (paged KV cache, virtual memory for KV)
  - Engine (model forward pass, LoRA application, sampling)
  - In-process LoRA training (candle/tch, runs on background thread)
  - Training shares the already-loaded model — no second copy in VRAM
  - Hot-swap: training thread writes new adapter weights, signals engine
```

## Repository

GitHub: https://github.com/ericflo/kiln (private during development, public at v0.1.0)

Current state: Cargo workspace scaffolded with 5 crates, working scheduler with tests, mock engine, full HTTP API surface. All compiles and passes tests.

## Target Model

Qwen3.5-4B (hybrid Gated DeltaNet + GQA, 262K native context). 24 linear attention layers + 8 full attention layers. Only 8 layers need KV cache, so 128K context fits in ~4 GB.
The target model is Qwen3.5-4B. Period. Do NOT fall back to Qwen3-4B, do NOT suggest Qwen3-4B, do NOT create tasks for Qwen3-4B. The Gated DeltaNet linear attention layers MUST be implemented — that is the critical path, not a reason to switch models.

### Gated DeltaNet: IMPLEMENTED ✓
GDN was implemented in PR #19 and verified working on GPU. All 32 layers (24 GDN + 8 full attention) produce coherent output. E2E GPU tests pass with correct answers, haiku generation, and scientific explanations.
